We provide a TRIPOD+AI-mapped checklist, a benchmark specification and a research agenda.
comments: 20 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables; supplementary material (26 pages) in ancillary files. Data and code: https://github.com/abdul-raheem-shahzad/ml-ivf-live-birth-review. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence

paper_title: Climate Risk in Agriculture: An Integrative Review of Assessment, Impacts, Adaptation, and Institutions
paper_abstract: Few economic sectors are as exposed to climate variability and change as agriculture, and global food demand is still rising. Assessing agricultural climate risk is challenging because studies examine different impacts across spatial and temporal scales, limiting direct comparison. This integrative review organizes the literature around that problem in five domains. Climate risk arises when a physical hazard acts on exposed and vulnerable farms, crops, or people. It is not the same as the hazard itself, the realized impact, or resilience. Assessment methods range from crop models, statistical and threshold-based approaches, and spatial maps to surveys and financial metrics, and they are applied from the household to the continental scale under observed or future climatic conditions. Impacts extend from yield and livestock losses to lower farm income, weaker credit quality, and reduced food access, and they include compound heat–drought and flood sequences. Farmers’ decisions depend on risk perception, risk tolerance, and access to labor, finance, water, and information. Responses include agronomic adjustments, climate-smart practices, insurance, credit, and, when incremental measures prove insufficient, broader changes to production systems. Whether these responses can be scaled up depends on policy, public capacity, climate services, and spatial targeting. Rather than pooling heterogeneous effect sizes or ranking practices globally, this review identifies differences in empirical metrics and bottlenecks that constrain farm-level implementation.

paper_title: Organisational Resilience in Medical Rehabilitation During Pandemics and Comparable Crises: A Nationwide Survey of Facility Managers in Germany
paper_abstract: Maintaining rehabilitation services during pandemics is an international preparedness challenge. This study examines organisational responses and support needs in Germany as a national case example. A nationwide cross-sectional survey of outpatient and inpatient rehabilitation facility managers was conducted online and by post between June and September 2021. Of 599 returned questionnaires, 535 were included in the analysis. Closed-ended responses were analysed descriptively, and open-ended responses using qualitative content analysis. Overall, 13.6% of facilities reported poor or very poor preparedness, while 38.8% reported good or very good preparedness. Establishing separate staff teams was particularly challenging, with 50.8% rating implementation as problematic or very problematic. Managers reported that information sharing, consistent communication, adapted workflows, testing and hygiene measures had worked well. Clear and nationally consistent requirements were the most frequently mentioned need when reflecting on support that would have helped during the pandemic. Financial support and clear guidance remained important at the time of the survey. The findings highlight organisational, communication and resource-related factors in maintaining rehabilitation care. This German case offers context-specific lessons for integrating rehabilitation into broader pandemic preparedness and crisis planning.

paper_title: Molecular Tumor Boards and Access to Therapeutic Cancer Trials Worldwide: A Scoping Review Protocol
paper_abstract: Introduction: Molecular tumor boards (MTBs) interpret molecular findings and connect patients with cancer to therapeutic options, including clinical trials. A recent European scoping review examines MTB implementation, while earlier global reviews address treatment attrition and clinical effectiveness. This scoping review will map global evidence on MTB-supported access to therapeutic trials and subsequent participation, including pathways, barriers, facilitators, and gaps across geographical and economic settings. Methods: The review will follow Arksey and O’Malley’s five core stages, incorporating selected refinements from Levac and colleagues and JBI guidance. Review and search reporting will follow PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S, respectively. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, and APA PsycINFO will be searched from inception, supplemented by citation and targeted grey literature searches. Searches will combine MTB and oncology terminology without requiring enrollment or outcome terms. No date, geographical, country-income, or language restrictions will apply. Eligible empirical sources will describe an MTB and provide substantive information on at least one therapeutic-trial access or participation stage, barrier, or facilitator. Neither a complete patient pathway nor a measured enrollment outcome will be required. Two reviewers will independently screen titles, abstracts, and full texts. A charting form will be piloted on at least five sources; one reviewer will chart each source, and a second will verify all entries. Results and Analysis: Descriptive and narrative synthesis will map countries, income groups, MTB models, trial identification, matching, referral, screening, enrollment, and subsequent participation. Country income and reported local resources will be recorded separately. Counts, denominators, matching definitions, follow-up periods, and evidence sources will be retained. Treatment initiation, withdrawal, discontinuation, and completion will be mapped when reported; response and survival will provide secondary context. Findings will identify evidence gaps and approaches that may inform future UAE pathways. Ethics and Dissemination: Ethics approval is not anticipated because the review will use publicly available information without collecting identifiable participant data. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, professional meetings, and a practical evidence summary.

paper_title: Micronutrient Status in Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Oral Carcinogenesis: A Scoping Review of Mechanistic Pathways and Evidence Gaps
paper_abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with a modestly higher risk of oral cancer (OC) in crude analyses, while micronutrient deficiencies affect approximately 45% of people with T2DM. Several micronutrients linked to oral carcinogenesis—vitamin D, folate, vitamin B12, zinc, selenium, magnesium, and iron—are also among those most depleted in diabetes. Despite this overlap, only four published studies have assessed micronutrient status or intake, glycemic status, and an oral cancer or precancer outcome in the same participants, and none has reported incidence. Conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR, this scoping review brings together three related evidence streams (diabetes–OC epidemiology, micronutrient–OC epidemiology, and micronutrient status in diabetes). It also catalogs the direct three-way evidence, maps converging molecular pathways, outlines expected mechanistic differences between type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and T2DM and proposes study designs to test the interaction. Three findings temper the conventional interpretation of this triad. The association between T2DM and oral cancer is no longer significant after adjusting for smoking, alcohol and adiposity. Areca nut contributes to both diabetes and oral cancer, making it a shared cause rather than a covariate. In addition, three Mendelian randomization analyses find no causal effect of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D, HbA1c, insulin-like growth factor 1 or adiposity on oral or oropharyngeal cancer. The triad is therefore mechanistically coherent but epidemiologically weak once confounding is addressed; for the exposures most often proposed, causal designs have already tested and not supported the link. What remains still open is a narrower, more tractable question: micronutrient status in oral cohorts that distinguish diabetes type and record areca nut (betel nut) use at the individual level. The distinction between T1DM and T2DM, routinely collapsed in the existing literature, is the one element of the hypothesis that current causal evidence supports—and the one for which observational data are entirely absent.

paper_title: Multimodal Reasoning, Agentic Systems, and Embedding Models: A Survey of Recent Advances
paper_abstract: Multimodal models increasingly reason over what they perceive, act in digital and physical environments, and retrieve content across modalities. This survey reviews recent advances in the three families of models behind these abilities: multimodal reasoning models, which reach answers through chains of thought trained with reinforcement learning; multimodal agentic systems, which run such models in a loop of perception, reasoning and action with tools, graphical interfaces, robots and search engines; and multimodal embedding models, which map images, text, audio, video and documents into a shared space for retrieval and memory. We present them in one mathematical framework in which every model composes modality encoders, a connector and a foundation-model backbone ending in a generative or an embedding head. Within it we trace reasoning from attention-based visual question answering to group-relative policy optimization and ``thinking with images''; agents from tool-augmented programs to GUI, embodied and search agents trained with verifiable rewards; and embeddings from canonical correlation analysis and contrastive encoders (CLIP, SigLIP) to instruction-following universal embedders. More than 350 works are organized along five taxonomies, and we summarize benchmarks and reported results and close with open problems, including the perception bottleneck, faithful reasoning, agent safety, efficiency and evaluation.

paper_title: Interdental Cleaning and Digital Support in Community Periodontal Prevention: A Narrative Review and Proposed Implementation Framework
paper_abstract: Background: Periodontal prevention requires effective daily plaque control, individualized risk management, and timely access to professional care. Interdental cleaning is a core self-care measure, while digital services may support education, communication, and referral. Evidence for these approaches differs substantially, and digital engagement should not be equated with clinical benefit. Objective: To synthesize selected evidence on interdental cleaning, mobile health, teledentistry, and artificial-intelligence-assisted periodontal assessment, and to propose a cautious community implementation framework. Review approach: This narrative review draws on selected clinical guidelines, policy documents, systematic and scoping reviews, and relevant primary studies. A targeted, non-systematic literature update was undertaken through 1 November 2026. The review was not designed to be exhaustive or reproducible; no formal risk-of-bias assessment or quantitative synthesis was conducted. Synthesis: Interdental device choice should reflect anatomy, periodontal status, dexterity, preference, and atraumatic access. Interdental brushes are recommended when anatomically feasible, particularly in periodontal maintenance; floss may be considered for contacts that cannot be safely accessed with a brush. Mobile applications and reminders may support selected behaviors, but recent evidence includes null findings in periodontal-care and older-adult settings, and results from orthodontic populations should not be generalized. Teledentistry can facilitate communication and triage but does not replace a comprehensive periodontal examination. AI tools require task-specific validation, transparent reporting, and human oversight. Conclusion: A community approach can link individualized interdental self-care with accessible education, appropriate referral, optional digital follow-up, and staged evaluation of new technologies. The proposed framework is conceptual and has not been tested; its feasibility, effectiveness, equity, and cost require prospective evaluation.

paper_title: A Bibliometric Analysis of CT Image Segmentation for Liver Cancer Screening Using Artificial Intelligence (1998--2026): A Review
paper_abstract: Liver cancer is a global challenge, with increasing mortality rates. This article presents a detailed bibliometric analysis of the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) methods to segment CT images and, subsequently, screen for liver cancer. We analyzed 2029 articles indexed in the recognized Scopus database, which covers the period between 1998 and 2026 (data collected on July 25, 2026), using a bibliometric analysis and visualization software called VOSviewer, in combination with complementary network analysis methods to explore co-occurrence networks, authors' scientific performance, and influence on citations. Major findings include the identification of researchers, research organizations, and countries contributing to the development of AI-based liver cancer screening techniques, with China, India, and the United States being the main contributors. Similarly, our study highlights the most influential publications and journals in this field, and also the accelerated increase in research output after 2019, mainly supported by deep learning algorithms. Five thematic clusters emerged from keyword co-occurrence analysis: clinical and radiomic evaluation, deep learning-based CT segmentation, quality imaging and contrast-enhanced imaging, neural networks, and AI applications in MRI-based oncology imaging. The analysis also highlights gaps in the existing and burgeoning literature for future investigations, most notably explainable AI, integration of multimodal imaging data, and testing in large-scale clinical settings.

paper_title: Employee Privacy and Human Review in AI Workplace Monitoring in Bangladesh
paper_abstract: Artificial intelligence can expand the ability of employers to collect and analyse information about work. Whether such monitoring is acceptable depends on both informational safeguards and the procedures through which monitoring data affect employees. This study examines expectations of notice, proportionate purpose, data disclosure and human review in Bangladesh. It analyses 385 adult respondents who reported awareness of AI, using item-level distributions, paired endorsement comparisons and an exploratory proportional-odds model. The sample includes 238 law students and is not presented as representative of employed workers or the national workforce. Notice that AI monitors workplace activity was endorsed by 292 respondents (75.8%), while review before serious employment consequences was endorsed by 205 (53.2%). Their within-person difference was 22.6 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval 16.4-28.8; Holm-adjusted p < .001). Sixty-one respondents (15.8%) endorsed all four procedural safeguards. Privacy safeguards were said to affect acceptance of monitoring by 301 respondents (78.2%). In the adjusted model, the notice expectation showed a pointwise odds ratio of 1.35 (95% confidence interval 1.04-1.75), but its Holm-adjusted p-value was .102; the four focal associations therefore provide limited evidence after multiplicity adjustment. These findings describe distinctions between stated expectations, not the effect of actual monitoring, privacy violations or psychological-contract breach. Integrating legal safeguards with job demands-resources and psychological-contract perspectives, the article proposes a sequence connecting notice, purpose limitation, usable information and meaningful review. Longitudinal and experimental studies of employees and implemented systems are needed to examine whether these safeguards change perceived privacy and workplace outcomes.

paper_title: Current Advances in the Management of Gout: From Uric Acid Targets to Emerging Therapies-Narrative Review
paper_abstract: Gout is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis and results from persistent hyperuricemia leading to deposition of monosodium urate crystals within joints and soft tissues. Although conventional urate-lowering therapy remains effective for most patients, suboptimal adherence, delayed dose escalation, intolerance, and refractory disease continue to limit long-term disease control. Contemporary management has shifted toward a treat-to-target (T2T) strategy that aims to achieve and maintain serum urate concentrations below the saturation threshold to promote crystal dissolution and prevent recurrent flares, tophus formation, and structural joint damage. Recent advances have expanded therapeutic options through selective urate transporter inhibitors, next-generation xanthine oxidase inhibitors, engineered uricase formulations, immune tolerance platforms, biologic therapies targeting the IL-1 pathway, and novel NLRP3 inflammasome inhibitors. Emerging evidence also supports the potential urate-lowering and cardiometabolic benefits of sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, while advances in proteomics, metabolomics, and transcriptomics have identified promising biomarkers that may improve diagnosis, disease monitoring, and precision medicine approaches. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on treat-to-target strategies, established urate-lowering therapies, emerging pharmacologic agents, biologic therapies, and novel biomarkers, and highlights future directions that may facilitate individualized management of gout.

paper_title: Reasoning for Generation, Generation for Reasoning: A Survey of Unified Multimodal Models
paper_abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) integrate visual understanding and image generation, creating the opportunity for each capability to strengthen the other. However, architectural unification does not guarantee such interaction: models frequently understand visual requirements that they fail to realize in generated images, and generate intermediate images that their reasoning does not use. This survey examines both directions of transfer and why each remains challenging. We review the architectural foundations and representative model families, and the tasks in which understanding and generation must interact. For understanding → generation, we organize methods into training-free approaches that improve inference with frozen components and training-based approaches that learn reasoning, alignment, verification, or refinement, and compare them by stage of intervention, required access, and computational cost. For generation → reasoning, we review visual-imagination methods that reason with generated images, latent visual tokens, geometric representations, drawing tools, or external world models. We further examine evaluation protocols that distinguish individual task performance, cross-modal consistency, and genuine synergy. Across both directions, a shared challenge emerges: a correct intermediate, whether a reasoning trace or an imagined image, is not necessarily used. We conclude with open problems in reasoning-to-generation alignment, verifiable imagination, reliable self-correction, and compute-matched evaluation.

paper_title: A Comprehensive Survey of 4D Gaussian Splatting for Dynamic Scene Reconstruction
paper_abstract: 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) has rapidly become a prominent approach to dynamic scene reconstruction and free-viewpoint rendering, inheriting the explicit primitives and real-time rasterization of 3D Gaussian splatting while adding a temporal axis. Although 4DGS is a nascent area of research, the number of methods has grown explosively, making it difficult to navigate. In this paper, we survey recent progress in 4DGS. Specifically, we cover three major themes: (i) representations, organized into deformation-based, native 4D-primitive, hybrid/decomposition, anchor/stream- ing, and feed-forward/generalizable families; (ii) compression and storage efficiency, the defining practical bottleneck of 4DGS; (iii) applications, including autonomous driving, 4D content generation, editing and semantics, event and constrained capture, and avatars/robotics/medicine. We also present comparative results on widely used benchmarks, together with observations and future research directions. A taxonomy and chronological overview of representative methods are provided throughout this survey to help readers situate individual works.

paper_title: Regulation of MicroRNA Biogenesis and Its Implications in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis: A Narrative Review
paper_abstract: Background: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive, and fatal interstitial lung disease characterized by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix and progressive destruction of the lung architecture. Repeated epithelial injury and aberrant tissue repair are strongly associated with its pathogenesis; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression remain incompletely understood. Altered microRNA (miRNA) expression has been extensively associated with IPF, but comparatively little attention has been given to the mechanisms regulating miRNA maturation and processing during pulmonary fibrosis. Objective: In this narrative review, we aimed to describe the relationship between IPF pathogenesis and alterations in miRNA maturation, with particular emphasis on post-transcriptional mechanisms that may disrupt the production and function of mature miRNAs. Methods: We conducted a narrative review of the available literature using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. No specific time frame was established because of the limited number of studies directly addressing miRNA maturation in IPF. Original research articles were prioritized, while relevant studies describing miRNA maturation mechanisms in other biological and disease contexts were also considered to provide mechanistic insight. Results: The available evidence suggests that alterations in miRNA maturation may contribute to miRNA dysregulation in IPF beyond changes in transcriptional control. Disruption of the Drosha/DGCR8 microprocessor complex, altered Dicer-dependent processing, and post-transcriptional modifications of miRNA precursors may affect the production of mature miRNAs. In addition, adenosine-to-inosine editing mediated by adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) may modify miRNA sequences and influence their maturation, stability, and target selection. Mechanotransduction-associated pathways, including Hippo/YAP signaling, may further interfere with the miRNA-processing machinery. These alterations may contribute to the persistent dysregu-lation of antifibrotic miRNAs, including miR-29, thereby promoting extracellular matrix accumulation and sustaining profibrotic signaling. Conclusions: Although evidence directly linking defects in miRNA maturation to IPF remains limited, available findings support the hypothesis that alterations in post-transcriptional miRNA processing represent an additional regulatory layer contributing to pulmonary fibrosis. Further experimental studies are needed to determine how specific alterations in miRNA maturation and editing contribute to IPF pathogenesis and whether components of the miRNA-processing machinery may represent potential therapeutic targets.

paper_title: Smart Tech, Smart Tourists: A Systematic Review of Digital Technology and Sustainable Tourist Behaviour
paper_abstract: Tourists are increasingly using digital technologies to search for, book, stay and share about their experiences. Their environmental concern is generally not reflected in their actual travel behaviour. Digital technologies are increasingly influencing tourist decisions, but it is not clear whether they actually close the gap between pro-environmental attitudes and pro-environmental behaviour. This review looks at the mechanisms by which digital technologies can lead to changes in sustainable tourist behaviour, the strength of the evidence for each mechanism and when individual change results in net benefit at the system level. Following PRISMA 2020, we identify the digital mechanisms which lead to changes in sustainable tourist behaviour and assess the strength of the evidence for each. Scopus and Web of Science were searched for studies published between 2010 and 30 June 2026 with a supplementary citation search. A total of 156 studies were included and coded by touchpoint, design and outcome. They were graded for strength of evidence and synthesised thematically. The literature is very new with 95% of the studies published since 2020 and the vast majority (87%) reporting on stated intentions. Only 11 of the studies actually looked at a change in behaviour; these are largely field experiments in which the technology influenced behaviour at the moment of choice via real time feedback, digital defaults, recommenders, robot delivered prompts or app based rewards. Evidence for the use of social media, labels, immersive media and smart destinations is still emerging. AI agents can either promote or inhibit pro-environmental behaviour. Spillover, rebound and the technology’s own footprint are rarely measured. We propose a Technology-Mediated Sustainable Tourist Behaviour (TMSTB) model which links behavioural to system level outcomes and which sets six questions for future research.

paper_title: Beyond the Dedicated Suite: A Practical Review of Shared Imaging Platforms for Precision Interventional Pulmonology
paper_abstract: Background: Advanced interventional pulmonology (IP) increasingly depends on cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and hybrid imaging workflows for the diagnosis and management of intrapulmonary lesions. However, globally, many IP teams still lack a dedicated pulmonology procedure suite in their institution and instead perform cases in rooms originally designed for cardiovascular, neurovascular, interventional radiology, or surgical use. Methods: This review evaluates ceiling-mounted single-plane systems, floor-mounted systems, older and newer biplane angiography suites, robotic CBCT hybrid operating room systems and mobile CBCT systems and their suitability for IP procedures. Results: Based on available literature and institutional experience, ceiling-mounted single-plane systems may offer ergonomic advantages for bronchoscopic IP because they preserve head-side access and procedural ergonomics. Floor-mounted systems remained usable, particularly in older institutions, but could restrict airway-side positioning. Biplane-suite capabilities varied by system generation and configuration; some newer configurations provided CBCT and overlay functions that may facilitate pulmonary workflows. Robotic hybrid systems may provide broad procedural flexibility for complex and combined procedures but require greater institutional support. Mobile CBCT systems represented a practical entry strategy for centers without dedicated infrastructure, while conventional multidetector CT remained valuable for selected percutaneous interventions. Successful adaptation across all platforms depended on room layout, workstation capability, team familiarity, anesthesia support, and multidisciplinary collaboration. Conclusions: Advanced IP programs can be developed without a purpose-built pulmonology suite. Careful adaptation of existing imaging environments may allow centers to expand precision bronchoscopic and percutaneous capabilities according to local resources and workflow realities.

paper_title: Integrating Machine Learning and Uncertainty Quantification for Real-Time Decision-Making in Digital Twins: A System-Centric Review and Perspective
paper_abstract: Digital Twins are evolving from passive virtual representations into closed-loop systems that continuously synchronize with physical assets and drive real-time decisions. Yet predictive modeling, machine learning (ML), uncertainty quantification (UQ), and decision-making have been studied as separate capabilities, leaving limited understanding of their integration and maintenance during online operation. This narrative review, scoped by the functional requirements of real-time decision-making rather than by Digital Twin terminology alone, examines how such decisions are generated and sustained in engineering Digital Twins. We first examine foundational decision-making architectures and representative engineering applications, followed by methods that address their limitations across the decision loop. We identify optimization-based, policy-based, and knowledge-based approaches as the major pathways from virtual representation to action. Across them, ML plays three roles in decision-making: enabling efficient surrogate modeling, transforming heterogeneous physical feedback into decision-relevant information, and accelerating or directly generating decisions. UQ supports uncertainty-aware decisions and model adaptation, while continual validation, drift detection, and adaptation help maintain reliable operation as the physical system evolves. Together, these findings underscore the need for a shift from a model-centric to a system-centric perspective on Digital Twins, where its performance depends on the interactions with sensing, state estimation, computation, decision-making, and adaptation rather than on their standalone performance. Therefore, future research should shift from isolated algorithm development toward system-level co-design, scalable decision-making, and approaches to design, and data-efficient continual adaptation and validation for AI-enabled autonomous systems.

paper_title: COSMIO: A Benchmark for Cross-Survey Modality Imputation
paper_abstract: Large-scale astronomical surveys define a heterogeneous, partially observed multi-survey learning setting: each object is observed by only a subset of surveys, while survey observations differ in resolutions, wavelength coverage, noise characteristics, and footprints. This setting gives rise to a natural machine learning problem: given observations of an object in some surveys, how to infer its appearance in other surveys. We formalize this as the problem of cross-survey modality imputation and introduce COSMIO, a multi-survey benchmark of aligned observations obtained by forward-rendered shared astrophysical scenes across LSST, Euclid, and Roman under survey-specific instrument characteristics. The benchmark enables systematic evaluation of imputation across source-target survey combinations and missing-survey patterns. We evaluate a broad range of machine learning methods for imputation, which reveal a clear domain gap: methods developed for existing imputation settings transfer poorly to the survey setting. We identify rare-event imputation as a central challenge. This regime arises in the early stages of new surveys, when rare but scientifically valuable phenomena may be available only from prior surveys. We use strong gravitational lensing, where light from a background galaxy is gravitationally deflected by a foreground galaxy, as a representative rare-event setting. We evaluate model performance on zero-shot imputation of gravitational lenses and on downstream scientific tasks using the imputed lens observations. On our constructed evaluation set of galaxy-galaxy strong lenses, performance degrades under rare-event distribution shift, and this degradation further propagates to the downstream lens-detection task. Code: https://github.com/fw-ic/COSMIO.

paper_title: Can Large Language Models Review the Scientific Literature? A Test Against a 102-Article Benchmark
paper_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support scientific literature reviews, yet evaluations often examine individual tasks rather than the review process as a whole. We assess six AI tools across four stages: finding relevant articles, interpreting them, synthesizing across them, and proposing future research. The benchmark is a published review of the Spanish plume weather pattern and its 102-article corpus.   In the initial searches, five tools collectively identified 57 articles, with the best individual tool finding 42. Institutional library access increased discovery from 42 to 82 articles for Codex and from 15 to 79 for Claude Code. Given the complete corpus of 102 PDFs, three tools correctly identified all 18 articles discussing the Spanish plume substantially, but incorrectly classified 40% to 79% of the 84 passing mentions as substantial. The same three tools produced syntheses evaluated blindly by two domain experts. Although largely accurate, the syntheses provided limited insight and sometimes contained unsupported claims, quotation errors, and exaggerated statements of consensus. Finally, all three tools proposed research directions broader than the Spanish plume literature, although two approached questions identified in the benchmark review.   No single tool performed best across all tasks. We provide eight recommendations for researchers using AI tools in literature reviews. Our findings suggest that LLMs can assist with discovering and interpreting scientific literature, particularly when institutional access is available, but cannot replace expert judgment in evaluating evidence or synthesizing research.
comments: 34 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Data, prompts, analysis scripts and results: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23849039 (GitHub: https://github.com/abx40/spanish-plume-llm-literature-review)

paper_title: KG-AST for Cheaper CI/CD: Budgeted Test Selection and AI Bug Review
paper_abstract: Continuous integration and AI-assisted review spend the same budget on every commit, although few commits introduce bugs. We study KG-AST, which scores each commit risk from git history and code-graph features before heavy tests or AI review run, so the budget goes to the riskiest commits first, and which hands the AI reviewer only a graph slice around the change. On 155 open-source projects in 11 languages, a single cross-language model trained on other projects ranks commits so that heavy testing of the riskiest 20% covers 49-64% of bug-introducing commits depending on the language, against 20% for random selection and 40-55% for testing the biggest change first.   Every language beats the biggest-change baseline, by 3.8 to 13.2 points. In 20 Java projects the gain at a 20% budget is 15.1 points (64.6% vs 49.5%, 95% interval +11.6 to +18.4), and the model wins in 19 of the 20 projects. About twelve training projects suffice; richer features, tuning and cleaner labels did not help. An AI reviewer that sees only a commit's diff finds 26% of later-fixed defects exactly (32% with graph context), and about half of its findings that did not match a later fix were judged real by independent AI judges. A static call-graph selector runs about 8% of a test suite while including a test written for the fix in 85% of 67 fix commits. The Poincare embedding used in our retrieval work adds nothing measurable here: commit-risk AUC, bug review and severity ranking are unchanged or worse. The labels are noisy and the budget metric assumes a heavy test catches the bug it covers; no CI minutes were measured.

paper_title: From Prediction to Control: A Survey of Closed-Loop World Models for Robot Learning
paper_abstract: World models are now used throughout robot learning: to shape policy representations, generate training data, score behavior, plan actions and correct execution. Yet the field has not converged on what such a model should predict, what it should be conditioned on, what data it should learn from, or how it should compute. We argue that this lack of convergence is expected. A world model helps a robot only through the component that uses its predictions, such as a learner, a planner, an evaluator or a controller, so the quality of a model is relative to that consumer: the same predictive error can be harmless when generating offline training data and decisive when a planner ranks actions under a control deadline. Starting from a first-order account of how model errors reach the robot’s real-world return, we organize the literature along the path from prediction to control. On the model side, we characterize world models by four design dials (prediction space, conditioning, knowledge source and computation), each embodying a fundamental trade-off. On the consumer side, we identify five pathways through which predictions change behavior: as features, as generated experience, as scores, as decision-time futures of candidate actions, and as residuals between prediction and observation. We then relate these pathways to the learning regimes and policies that consume them, to the requirements of different embodiments, and to evaluation protocols that measure utility on real robots. Finally, we review how deployment data close the outer loop by refitting models and policies, and we cast open problems as unresolved trade-offs on the design dials. We maintain a companion repository that organizes the surveyed works by section.

paper_title: Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART) Affects Salivary Biomarkers in Persons Living with HIV (PLWH) and Periodontal Disease: A Narrative Review
paper_abstract: HIV infection and antiretroviral therapy (ART) both alter the composition of saliva, which is easy to collect. This narrative review examined whether salivary biomarkers differ in persons living with HIV (PLWH) receiving ART, with and without periodontal disease (PD). We searched Pub-Med, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar and Google Scholar for articles published between January 2010 and July 2026 and included 14 studies. Compared with HIV-negative controls, PLWH had lower salivary flow, sodium, chloride and uric acid, higher calcium and IgA, and more oxidative stress. Protein and electrolyte levels differed by ART status, and oral bacteria differed between ART regimens. Citric acid accumulated at low CD4+ T-cell counts, and metabolite profiles shifted after ART was started. Salivary Torque teno virus and several bacterial and fungal genera tracked CD4+ counts. Human β-defensin-2 (hBD-2) and secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor varied with ART status and duration. hBD-2 was associated with PD in HIV-negative individuals but not in PLWH, whereas salivary miR-324-5p tracked periodontal inflammation in PLWH on ART. Most studies were small and cross-sectional, and none identified a consistent ART-specific profile. Saliva could help monitor immune status and treatment response in PLWH, but longitudinal studies with standardized periodontal assessment are needed first.

paper_title: The Battle for Township Economic Resources: State Power, Informal Economic Governance and the Struggle for Control in South Africa's Townships: A Systematic Review
paper_abstract: Introduction: Township economies are shaped by interactions among state authorities, informal traders, community organisations and other local economic actors. The supplied literature links informal economic activity to livelihood support, institutional exclusion, community governance and contested implementation, but provides limited direct evidence about South African township resource control.Methods: The researcher-selected databases and information sources were Google Scholar and ERIC. The eligibility protocol restricted publication years to 2018–2026. The exact calendar date of search execution was not recorded in the verified identification provenance; this is distinct from the publication-year eligibility range. A systematic review was undertaken using Google Scholar and ERIC, with eligibility restricted to English-language publications from 2018–2026. The exact Boolean strategy, inclusion and exclusion criteria, PRISMA workflow, CASP appraisal and COSTAQDA-supported thematic synthesis were documented.Results: The evidence presents informal activity as economically valuable while reflecting restricted access to formal finance, infrastructure, predictable pricing and administrative procedures. Governance responses tend toward managed inclusion through simplified documentation, designated trading spaces and combined formal–informal arrangements. Community governance appears more accountable when supported by rights documents, constitutions, revenue procedures, financial rules and defined roles, but formal recognition does not ensure implementation or participation. These conclusions are primarily transferable observations because the extracted evidence contains very limited direct evidence from South African townships.Discussion/Conclusion: State and informal governance mechanisms appear capable of structuring access to resources, but the review cannot establish how they redistribute control within South African township economies. Stronger township-specific empirical research is required before definitive policy or causal conclusions can be drawn.

paper_title: Explainable AI Driven Frameworks for Real Time Cyber Threat Detection and Response: A Systematic Review
paper_abstract: The digitization of an ever-developing network of cybersecurity threats has weighted traditional packet filter rule-based firewalls and signature based intrusion detection systems towards being less effective against zero day vulnerabilities, ransomware, polymorphic malware, and Advanced Persistent Threat (APTs) attacks. Emerging technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have potential to be game changers for proactive and adaptive defence of cyberspace. This review investigates AI powered cybersecurity systems: machine learning algorithms, deep learning architectures, Reinforcement Learning, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). Also investigated will be applications within Cloud Computing, Healthcare, Maritime Systems and National Critical Infrastructure. Further discussions will include feature engineering, Transformer based Zero Shot Learning (ZSL), SOAR integration, blockchain-based forensic integrity, adversarial AI and quantum computing concerns. The results demonstrated positive trends through AI powered cybersecurity systems improving detection Accuracy, lowering False Positives, reducing incident response time and enhancing Autonomous Defence capabilities. However, challenges around Explainability, Ethical Governance, Scalability of Computation, and Adversarial Resistance are expressed as possible major concerns. A conclusion point will outlining future research directions to develop, build and maintain resilient, transparent and quantum resistant Cybersecurity Ecosystems.

paper_title: End-Edge-Cloud Collaborative Inference for Efficient Large Language Model Services: A Survey
paper_abstract: As large language model (LLM) services expand toward distributed environments characterized by latency sensitivity, heterogeneous resources, and stringent privacy constraints, neither end-only nor cloud-only deployment can simultaneously balance generation quality, response latency, resource cost, and energy consumption. This survey systematically reviews optimization techniques for end-edge-cloud collaborative LLM inference services and establishes a four-layer taxonomy encompassing the algorithm, model, system, and chip levels. This taxonomy captures the end-to-end execution chain from collaborative decision-making to physical execution. The algorithm layer determines inference paths and task partitioning; the model layer provides deployable and collaborative model forms; the system layer manages resource mapping and pipeline execution; and the chip layer supplies the underlying computing, storage, and interconnect capabilities. These four layers are mutually dependent and collectively determine the end-to-end benefits of a collaborative solution. Furthermore, this survey defines representative collaboration paradigms and evaluation metrics, compares the performance gains, resource overheads, and applicability boundaries of different methods, and summarizes promising future directions, including cross-layer collaboration, dynamic adaptation, state-centric runtimes, and service-aware hardware.

paper_title: Institutional Overlap and the Politics of Accountability: A Systematic Review of Concurrent Parliamentary and Judicial Inquiries in South Africa
paper_abstract: Introduction: Concurrent parliamentary and judicial inquiries are intended to strengthen accountability, yet overlapping investigative arrangements may also fragment responsibility, divert resources and weaken implementation. The supplied literature provides relevant evidence on South African commissions of inquiry, public-sector governance and municipal accountability, but offers limited direct evidence on simultaneous parliamentary and judicial investigations. Methods: The researcher-selected databases and information sources were Google Scholar, ERIC, OpenAlex and Crossref. The eligibility protocol restricted publication years to 2015–2026. COSTAQDA recorded source-level retrieval through OpenAlex (150 retrieved; 319 available), Crossref (150 retrieved; 691 available). Where researcher-selected sources did not expose a suitable direct bulk-search connector, COSTAQDA used its OpenAlex/Crossref discovery bridge while preserving the researcher-selected source names in the PRISMA record. The identification run recorded 300 records before cross-source deduplication and 298 unique records after deduplication. Results: Six codes, three categories and three analytical themes were developed. Institutional overlap expanded investigative capacity and public documentation but could reproduce fragmentation when existing enforcement systems remained unreformed. Repeated inquiries could displace prosecution and divert resources. Effective democratic oversight depended on institutional independence, professional capacity and implementation pathways. Direct South African evidence was sparse, and systematic comparative evidence on resource efficiency was absent. Discussion/Conclusion: Institutional overlap is neither intrinsically beneficial nor harmful. Its effects depend on whether overlapping mandates are coordinated with independent enforcement, clear responsibility and mechanisms that convert findings into sanctions or administrative change.

paper_title: From Euclid’s Compass to FEM meshing: An Instrumental Review of Mathematical Conventions and the Limits of Formal Logic
paper_abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive philosophical and historical critique of mathematical Platonism, arguing instead for an instrumentalist framework where mathematics evolves as an open-ended, highly adaptive sequence of pragmatic conventions driven by utility and the empirical demands of physical reality. By deconstructing foundational transitions across geometry, analysis, logic, and mathematical physics, we illustrate how mathematical rigour routinely relies on conceptual accommodations rather than a priori absolute truths. We begin by exposing a material paradox in Euclidean geometry: the physical act of constructing a circle via a compass violates Euclid’s Elements (c. 300 BC) definitions of dimensionless points and two-dimensional surfaces by piercing a three-dimensional substrate. Moving to projective geometry, we explore the visual and structural conventions of the vanishing point as an engineered fiction designed to satisfy the pragmatic utility of sight. In mathematical analysis, we examine how numerical approximations of transcendental constants—from Archimedes’ bounding of π to the modern proofs of transcendence for e (1873) and π (1882)—reveal a qualitative mutation where discrete rational sequences transform into irrational realities upon touching infinity, necessitating artificial axioms of completeness. Furthermore, we unpack the conceptual paradoxes of complex analysis, highlighting Euler’s arbitrary branch cuts designed to domesticate the multi-valued nature of the logarithm of negative numbers. We contextualize these foundational constraints through Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems (1931) and Turing’s Halting Problem (1936), demonstrating that formal systems cannot achieve closed autonomy and must look outward for new conventions when encountering unprovable truths. This dependency is mirrored in continuum mechanics, where Cauchy’s stress tensor (1827) introduced a nine-component algebraic entity born purely out of the physical necessity to couple force vectors with oriented surfaces, fracturing classical vector spaces to satisfy empirical constraints. Crucially, we extend this critique to computational fluid dynamics and field simulations, demonstrating how contemporary mesh-based solvers violently subvert the Eulerian assumption of mutually independent spatial and temporal variables, shackling them through the pragmatic constraints of the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) stability criterion. Finally, we deconstruct the relativism of numerical truth through modular arithmetic, tracing its formalization from Gauss’s Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801) to its contemporary manifestation in asymmetric cryptography (RSA, 1978). By demonstrating how the structural modulus shifts the output of basic operations, we illustrate that numbers are pliable symbols conforming to the spaces we construct for them. Ultimately, this essay conceptualizes mathematics as a fluid, dynamic conceptual technology whose validation and internal cohesion are dictated not by a transcendental realm, but by its instrumental utility in decoding and manipulating the physical universe.

paper_title: CR-Bench-v2: Evaluating the Real-World Utility of AI Code Review Agents
paper_abstract: The rapid growth of automated code generation has created a pressing need for automated code review. Yet code review resists full automation: it depends on context beyond the \textit{diff}, on the author's intent, and on judgments about design and maintainability on which even expert reviewers disagree. Existing code review benchmarks lack standardization and rely largely on noisy human review comments scored with text-similarity metrics, which reward surface overlap and fail to measure precision. We introduce \texttt{CR-Bench}, a defect-centric evaluation framework that recasts SWE-Bench issues as pull-request review tasks with full repository context. After filtering for review-detectable defects and grounding each to a single originating pull request, \texttt{CR-Bench} contains 584 instances, with a 174-instance \texttt{CR-Bench-Verified} subset derived from SWE-Bench Verified. Each instance pairs a pull request with a known defect, its ground-truth fix, and a taxonomy label for bug category, impact, and severity. We propose two complementary metrics: \emph{Known-Defect Detection Rate} (KDDR), which measures whether an agent identifies the labeled defect, and \emph{Usefulness Rate}, which measures the fraction of review comments that are actionable. We evaluate eight code review agents over four backbones, plus commercially available Gemini Code Assist, using three independent LLM judges. Even the strongest systems detect only about one-third of known defects (KDDR $\approx$ 33\%), and Gemini Code Assist detects 8.1\%.

paper_title: Rethinking B‐BBEE Policy Implementation: A Systematic Review of Regulatory Frameworks and Inclusive MSME Development in South Africa
paper_abstract: Introduction: Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (BBBEE) is intended to address apartheid-era exclusion through ownership, skills development, preferential procurement, enterprise development and wider economic participation. Its relationship with inclusive Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprise (MSME) development, growth and sustainability remains contested because access to benefits is uneven and implementation may privilege formal compliance over substantive transformation.Methods: The researcher-selected databases and information sources were Google Scholar, ERIC. The eligibility protocol restricted publication years to 2015–2026. The exact calendar date of search execution was not recorded in the verified identification provenance; this is distinct from the publication-year eligibility range. Google Scholar and ERIC were the researcher-selected information sources. The eligibility period was 2015–2026.Results: B-BBEE provides an inclusion-oriented policy route and can support finance, women’s empowerment, enterprise development and procurement access. However, benefits are conditional and uneven. Compliance burdens, regulatory instability, weak institutional capacity, fronting, corruption, elite capture and symbolic compliance constrain inclusive outcomes. Enterprise and supplier development are most promising when linked to capability building, meaningful operational participation, transparent procurement, finance, quality systems, long-term relationships and coordinated stakeholder support. Direct evidence on long-term MSME survival and micro-enterprise outcomes remains limited.Discussion/Conclusion: BBBEE is neither uniformly ineffective nor consistently developmental. Its contribution to inclusive MSME growth depends on whether regulatory compliance is connected to measurable, broad-based and sustainable productive outcomes. A reoriented framework should reduce navigational burdens, strengthen accountability and monitor enterprise-level outcomes rather than relying primarily on scorecard attainment.

paper_title: Artificial Intelligence and Sustainable Entrepreneurship in Territorial Innovation Ecosystems: A Scoping Review of Actors, Pathways and Gaps
paper_abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a lever for sustainable entrepreneurship and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), yet little is known about how its contribution unfolds within the territorial ecosystems where ventures emerge. This scoping review mapped how AI is conceptualised, its pathways, ecosystem actors, outcomes, risks and gaps. Following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR, we searched EBSCO Discovery Service, Lens.org and SciELO (2020–2026); AI-assisted screening and charting were fully verified, and two reviewers coded independently. Of 910 records, 26 studies were included. The evidence is recent (88% from 2025–2026) and concentrated in Europe and Asia; only three studies address Latin America. Of the 26 studies, 11 view AI through an instrumental lens, 10 through an infrastructural or orchestrating lens and 5 through an institutional lens. Sustainable business models (11), venture creation and ecosystem orchestration (10 each) were the most frequent pathways; governments and universities, the most frequent actors. Environmental effects were addressed in 15 studies but measured with an outcome indicator in only 2, and the SDGs cited were mainly economic and social (especially SDGs 8 and 9). We propose an integrative framework, research propositions and an agenda on causal designs, environmental measurement, AI governance and Latin America.

paper_title: Regulatory Compliance Requirements, Administrative Burden, Operational Costs and Compliance Efficiency Among SMEs: A Systematic Review
paper_abstract: Introduction: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) may experience regulatory compliance requirements as relatively high fixed costs because managerial time, documentation, specialist expertise and financial resources are limited. The supplied literature also suggests that simplification, digitalisation and proportionate regulation may improve compliance efficiency, although deregulation can create risks for oversight and public-interest protection.Methods: The researcher-selected databases and information sources were Google Scholar, ERIC. The eligibility protocol restricted publication years to 2015–2026. The exact calendar date of search execution was not recorded in the verified identification provenance; this is distinct from the publication-year eligibility range. Google Scholar and ERIC were the researcher-selected information sources for English-language peer-reviewed publications dated 2015–2026.Results: The synthesis generated seven codes, three categories, two descriptive themes and four analytical themes. Compliance was commonly associated with disproportionate administrative and financial burden, particularly where requirements were complex, fragmented, frequently changing or inconsistently enforced. Digital services, interoperable registers, automation, training and institutional support could reduce manual work and improve transparency, but their benefits depended on implementation capacity and system fit. Simplification and deregulation supported access and innovation in some contexts but required safeguards. Compliance could also improve formalisation, reporting accuracy, legitimacy and stakeholder assurance.Discussion/Conclusion: The evidence supports proportionate, risk-sensitive and coordinated compliance rather than deregulation alone. Policy effectiveness depends on regulatory coherence, institutional capability, SME knowledge, digital infrastructure, accessible guidance and meaningful consultation.

paper_title: Helleborus caucasifcus and Helleborus abchasicus: An Integrative Review of Taxonomy, Ecology, Phytochemical Diversity, and Conservation
paper_abstract: Helleborus caucasicus and Helleborus abchasicus are two Caucasian taxa of the family Ranunculaceae with considerable botanical, pharmacognostic, and phytochemical interest. However, knowledge of these plants remains fragmented across historical and contemporary publications, including a substantial body of literature published in Russian and Georgian, which limits its accessibility to the international scientific community. This narrative review synthesizes available evidence on their taxonomy, morphology, anatomical characteristics, distribution, ecology, phytochemical composition, biological activities, traditional uses, toxicity, and conservation. Attention is given to taxonomic uncertainties, intraspecific anatomical variability, and differences in research coverage between the two taxa. H. caucasicus has been more extensively investigated for steroidal constituents, including furostanol and spirostanol glycosides, caucasicosides A–M, ecdysteroids, and bufadienolides, whereas the phytochemistry of H. abchasicus remains comparatively underexplored. Studies of both species have also revealed complex lipid profiles influenced by plant organ, lipid class, and cultivation conditions. Available experimental evidence indicates cytotoxic and apoptosis-related effects of certain constituents of H. caucasicus, together with anti-inflammatory and wound-healing activities of lipid preparations from both species. Nevertheless, these findings remain predominantly preclinical, and species-specific toxicological evidence is insufficient. Conservation studies further reveal declining natural populations and variable outcomes of ex situ cultivation and reintroduction.

paper_title: Forward-Looking Information Disclosure: A Prisma-Based Systematic Literature Review
paper_abstract: The purpose of this systematic literature review (SLR) was to use the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework to systematically evaluate the literature on FLID and identify emerging research gaps. A systematic search was conducted in two major academic databases (Scopus & Web of Science) using predefined inclusion or exclusion criteria. The dominant theoretical frameworks identified are the Agency Theory and Impression Management Theory to explain the board's dual role to monitor and control agent behaviour while controlling and managing strategic representation through dissemination of future-oriented information and management of agency cost and information asymmetry. Other relevant theoretical frameworks include the Resource-Based View theory which provides insight into how internal resources affect FLID, Legitimacy theory which explains how stakeholder expectations affect FLID and Signalling theory which informs how information asymmetries influence FLID. The majority of previous studies on FLID were conducted in developed countries specifically in the United States. Research on this topic in developing countries such as Malaysia appears to be underrepresented. This study has identified several avenues for the potential use of alternative communication methods with respect to the examination of FLID in a post COVID-19 world that may include increased levels of uncertainty.

paper_title: Gate-Road Geomechanics in LTCC and Thick-Seam Longwall Mining: A Critical Review and Proposed Adaptive Framework for Indian Gondwana Coalfields
paper_abstract: Gate roadways provide access, ventilation, transport and services throughout longwall panel development and retreat. Their stability depends on stress orientation, roof-bed structure, discontinuities, pillar geometry, support response and extraction sequence. In longwall top-coal caving (LTCC), the deliberate fracture and rear-window drawing of upper coal add load-transfer interactions that are not represented by bottom-slice extraction or by high-cutting single-pass longwall. This critical narrative review synthesises published field studies, case histories, numerical analyses and technical literature relevant to LTCC and thick-seam gate-road behaviour, with particular attention to Indian Gondwana conditions. Adriyala is treated as a bottom-slice comparator: its retained upper coal informs roof behaviour and monitoring, but it is not evidence of deliberate LTCC top-coal drawing. The review proposes a six-stage adaptive framework linking site characterisation, extraction geometry, layout comparison, support design, installation verification, and monitoring-led updating. A TARP response logic is presented as a site-specific management tool. The framework is a structured synthesis of the reviewed evidence, not a validated design standard; numerical dimensions and support values from individual cases are not transferable without mine-specific analysis. Instrumented prospective studies in Indian thick-seam and LTCC panels are needed to test and refine the framework.

paper_title: The PATZi Protocol for Full-Arch Rehabilitation of the Atrophic Maxilla: A Narrative Review of the Literature
paper_abstract: Immediate, graftless full-arch rehabilitation of the atrophic maxilla is constrained by alveolar resorption, sinus pneumatization and poor posterior bone quality, and conventional four-implant configurations may end in a shortened dental arch, a long distal cantilever or an unplanned change of strategy during surgery. The PATZi protocol (Pterygoid, Anterior, Tilted, Zygomatic implants) was proposed in 2023 as a stepwise algorithm that sequences implant techniques by maxillary region, prefers the least invasive option in each region, reserves zygomatic implants for regions in which no other anchorage can be obtained, and codes each configuration to grade complexity and plan salvage. This narrative review outlines the protocol and appraises the evidence for each of its components. Systematic reviews report cumulative survival of roughly 92–96% for pterygoid implants, survival of tilted implants equivalent to that of axial implants and mean survival of 97% for zygomatic implants, whereas nasopalatine and transnasal anchorage rest largely on small series and case reports. Evidence on the protocol itself is limited to its original description, a one-year cohort of 142 immediately loaded arches with a Full-Arch Ratio of 94, a 2025 extension to the moderately atrophic maxilla and one case report. PATZi is a coherent, prosthetically driven framework, but prospective comparative studies with long-term follow-up are needed to establish its outcomes.

paper_title: Monitoring the Efficacy of Artemisinin-Based Combination Therapies in Angola: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Therapeutic Efficacy Studies
paper_abstract: Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are the cornerstone of treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in Angola. The Ministry of Health conducts therapeutic efficacy studies (TES) at sentinel sites to monitor treatment effectiveness and detect emerging antimalarial drug resistance. This study systematically reviewed the therapeutic efficacy and safety of ACTs used in Angola from 2006 to December 2025. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed to identify clinical studies evaluating the efficacy and safety of ACTs, including artemether-lumefantrine (AL), artesunate-amodiaquine (ASAQ), dihydroartemisininpiperaquine (DP) and artesunate-pyronaridine (ASPY), for the treatment of uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in Angola. Of 913 records identified, seven studies from Bengo, Benguela, Luanda, Lunda Sul, Uíge, and Zaire met the inclusion criteria. ACTs showed high therapeutic efficacy, with PCR-corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response (ACPR) generally exceeding 90% through 42 days of followup. However, AL efficacy was below 90% in Zaire in 2013, 2015, Lunda Sul in 2019, and Bengo in 2021, whereas AS-AQ and DP consistently maintained high efficacy. Molecular surveillance showed no evidence of established artemisinin resistance, although markers potentially associated with reduced lumefantrine susceptibility warrant continued monitoring. Adverse events were predominantly mild and transient. ACTs remain effective and well tolerated for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in Angola. Nevertheless, recurrent reductions in AL efficacy at specific sentinel sites highlight the need for sustained therapeutic efficacy and molecular surveillance through regular TES to enable early detection of emerging antimalarial resistance and inform national treatment policies.

paper_title: Perampanel, Lacosamide, Eslicarbazepine Acetate, and Brivaracetam in Adults Aged ≥65 Years with Epilepsy: A Narrative Review of Real‐World Evidence and Practical Prescribing Considerations
paper_abstract: Epilepsy prevalence sharply increases after age 65 years, but elderly adults are chronically underrepresented in key trials that form the licensing evidence base for antiseizure medications (ASMs), leaving clinicians to extrapolate from the experiences of younger cohorts. This narrative review aims to consolidate real-world evidence regarding the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of 4 commonly prescribed newer ASMs, perampanel (PER), lacosamide (LCM), eslicarbazepine acetate (ESL), and brivaracetam (BRV) among adults ≥65 years, provide pragmatic prescribing recommendations based on this evidence, and define key gaps where further study should be prioritized. Collating data from our structured search of observational cohorts, interventional trials and extensions, pooled and post hoc analyses, pharmacovigilance databases, and case series and reports, we found that reported effectiveness outcomes in older adults were generally comparable to those observed in broader adult populations, although heterogeneity across studies limits direct comparisons. ESL monotherapy produced 1-year retention rates of 72.7% and 6- and 12-month seizure freedom rates of 72.2% and 67.3% among patients ≥65 years; adjunctive LCM demonstrated superior seizure freedom rates among older versus younger patients (56.7% vs. 43.1%); and dedicated ≥65-year-old studies of ESL and BRV reaffirmed efficacy observed in overall populations, frequently at lower doses and slower titration schedules. Key safety signals were drug-specific: hyponatremia (more common and symptomatic in older adults) for ESL; dose-dependent PR interval prolongation and rare high-grade atrioventricular block/ventricular tachycardia, Brugada morphology, and sinus node dysfunction for LCM; and psychiatric or behavioral events, dose-dependent falls for PER. Evidence supported a class-wide relationship between chronic ASM exposure and falls and fractures, while a FAERS analysis found no significant drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) signal for BRV and analysis-dependent findings for LCM. In conclusion, newer ASMs are efficacious and generally well tolerated among older adults. However, optimized safe prescribing in this population requires ASM selection tailored to comorbidities, lower starting doses with slower titration, and drug-specific follow-up (e.g., serum sodium monitoring for ESL, cardiac conduction assessment for LCM, and behavior and fall risk assessment for PER). Evidence remains lacking in adults ≥65 years of age, particularly for brivaracetam.

paper_title: From PID to Reinforcement Learning in Building HVAC Control: A Control-Architecture Review of Tuning Strategies, Formulations, and Deployment Trade-offs
paper_abstract: This paper reviews control architectures for building heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, addressing the tension among energy demand, occupant comfort and equipment operability, and situating proportional-integral-derivative (PID) regulation within a layered control stack that also includes rule-based and model-based supervisory control and data-driven reinforcement learning (RL). It examines the thermostat-PID layer from two-position and scheduled setpoint control through proportional, PI and PID regulation and their tuning, then formulates RL for building control as a Markov decision process. Its central contribution is a taxonomy of where RL meets PID: RL as a gain tuner for an existing loop, as a direct replacement for the regulatory controller, as a hybrid with model predictive control, and as supervisory setpoint and schedule generation. Across these classes, the review establishes that the physical loop remains invariant while the intervention point changes, and that the classes differ in their requirements for actuation authority, state information, modelling, commissioning and constraint handling. It further establishes that PID is inexpensive and well codified but limited by nonlinearity, time variation, discrete mode switching, loop interaction and slow plant dynamics, while RL's admissible position must be argued rather than assumed. The paper concludes that these architectures are not competing philosophies of control but nested points of attachment on one HVAC plant, with hybrid implementations possible, and that deployment trade-offs must be assessed according to the specific control interface and scaffolding required.

paper_title: Semantic Interoperability in Federated Digital Twin Systems: A Systematic Review Through the Levels of Conceptual Interoperability Model
paper_abstract: When two companies connect their digital twins, software models of their plants kept up to date with live data, each twin must translate the other's data into its own terms, and that translation rule, called a mapping, can stop being correct when one company changes the meaning of its data without telling the other. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review screened 5,833 records and read 119 full texts to determine whether any published system detects such a broken mapping and repairs it while the twins operate. In all 32 included studies the mapping is fixed before operation, and the two ingredients of run-time repair appear only separately: cross-company matching without any check that the match still holds, and detection and repair of changed meaning within a single company. The review turns this gap into six requirements, each illustrated on one running example, that a system claiming run-time semantic interoperability between independently owned twins should meet.

paper_title: Reinforcement Learning in High-Energy Physics: A Survey from Accelerator Control to Theory Exploration
paper_abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm in which an agent learns a decision-making policy by interacting with an environment, guided by a scalar reward rather than explicit supervision. Supervised and unsupervised learning have become indispensable tools in high-energy physics (HEP), but they learn from fixed datasets, whereas many HEP tasks are closed-loop decisions: the data an algorithm observes depend on its choices, the feedback is sparse or delayed, and the objective is often measured on a real machine or in a stochastic simulation, not by a differentiable model. This survey reviews the application of RL to such tasks: accelerator control and feedback, data quality monitoring, jet grooming, clustering, and representation, charged particle tracking, beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) and string model building, detector design, trigger control, analysis, and formal quantum field theory computation. It provides a self-contained introduction to the underlying RL methods, from model-free and model-based to multi-agent, offline, inverse, and bandit approaches, reviews each domain against its traditional methods, and summarizes the head-to-head comparisons. The applications range from policies deployed on real accelerators and evaluated on recorded collision data to exploratory studies in formal theory. RL is most advantageous for repeated tasks with a fast simulator, decisions inside fast control loops, operation under faults and corrupted measurements, physics-based rewards in place of labels, and sequential discrete constructions with a reusable policy, while Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, and differentiable methods remain competitive elsewhere. We conclude with the open challenges that recur across domains, including reward design, sim-to-real transfer, safety, the lack of shared benchmarks, and the statistical validity of policy-driven decisions.

paper_title: AI-Aided and AI-Oriented Integrated Sensing, Communication, and Computation: A Survey
paper_abstract: The evolution from 5G to 6G networks marks a transition toward the "intelligence of everything." While 5G enables enhanced connectivity, 6G aspires to embed intelligence directly into communication infrastructures, creating systems that are adaptive, context aware, and capable of autonomous decision making. Realizing such systems depends on harmonizing three fundamental functions that compete for shared network resources and often pursue conflicting goals: (i) sensing for environmental and contextual information acquisition, (ii) communication for reliable and timely information exchange, and (iii) computation for information processing and decision making. This harmonization necessitates shifting from independent optimization to their joint design as a unified system, a paradigm known as Integrated Sensing, Communication, and Computation (ISCC). In parallel, AI has emerged both as an enabling tool for ISCC optimization and as a workload whose requirements influence ISCC system design. This survey comprehensively examines ISCC from this dual perspective by distinguishing between AI-aided ISCC, in which learning-based methods support the joint design and optimization of sensing, communication, and computation, and AI-oriented ISCC, in which these functions are jointly configured to support learning, inference, and distributed intelligence. The survey further examines the co-design of AI and ISCC, where AI requirements and ISCC constraints jointly shape system and model decisions. It further provides a comparative synthesis of the resulting design approaches, system architectures, performance metrics, and evaluation practices, relates these developments to application-specific requirements across different domains, and identifies open research problems toward scalable, adaptive, and trustworthy AI-ISCC systems.

paper_title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve
paper_abstract: The kernel of the Lean proof assistant checks that a proof establishes its statement. Whether the statement says what was intended is left to human reviewers. This is the old problem of validating a specification, and it grows more pressing as language models write formal statements in bulk and agents edit formal developments continuously. We present ProofPatch, a tool that helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid while the development changes. A reviewer can ask the kernel targeted questions about a statement, such as whether a hypothesis is needed or whether a counterexample exists. Each decision is stored with fingerprints of the statement as Lean elaborated it and of the definitions it depends on, and any declaration can be pinned so that a patch changing it is blocked, whether a person or an agent built on a large language model (LLM) wrote the patch. Working on elaborated terms rather than source text is the central design choice: notation and formatting changes leave a decision intact, and a changed definition reaches every theorem that uses it. On 229 pairs of consecutive revisions of Mathlib, Lean's mathematics library, ProofPatch sends 118 of 12,898 synthetic decisions back for review. Every text-based alternative misses at least 38 of these or sends back at least 13 times as many. On 1,527 labeled statements, kernel evidence flags unfaithful ones with precision 0.88 to 0.96, and in 344 runs of an LLM agent no change to a pinned statement got through.

paper_title: Change the Funnel, Not Who May Submit: Engineering Peer Review for the Flood
paper_abstract: Every reviewer knows the feeling: more papers each cycle, three full reviews for each of them, and a suspicion that near the accept line the outcome is luck. The numbers bear it out. NeurIPS received 30,709 submissions in 2026, more than three times as many as in 2021, and reviewing them took some 184,000 expert hours, or 92 years of researchers' time. Three-quarters of those hours went to papers that were rejected. And when NeurIPS twice had the same papers reviewed by two committees, the second rejected half of what the first accepted.   Conferences are responding by limiting who may submit. We simulated that answer, and an alternative, in a model calibrated to the NeurIPS experiments. The limits save little and select no better, and those based on a past acceptance fall mostly on new authors. The alternative changes how papers are judged, spending full reads only where a decision turns on them. In a staged funnel, an automated quality check first turns back papers that are not ready. The rest are ranked by their value, from short summaries, by readers that each submission brings. Only the finalists get a full read, which checks their claims and settles the final ranking. The staged funnel needs a little over half of today's expert hours, accepts 95.5% of papers in the top 3-10% (against 74% today), and makes nearly every top-0.5% paper a spotlight or oral. And because every paper brings its own reader, the funnel keeps pace with the flood.

paper_title: From White Canes to Edge AI: A Survey of Assistive Navigation Technologies for Blind and Low-Vision Individuals
paper_abstract: Independent mobility is a foundational requirement for the autonomy of blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals, yet the assistive technologies that support it have historically evolved slowly.
